lessons.title: Creating a Pitch Deck
lessons.body: A pitch deck is a short slide presentation that tells investors, partners, or lenders why your business is worth their money or support. In Africa, where many investors have limited time and see dozens of deals, your deck must be clear, visual, and compelling. Use 10-12 slides maximum. Start with a title slide: business name, your name, and a one-line description. Next, the problem slide: what pain are you solving? Use a real example, like 'Smallholder farmers in Kenya lose 30% of their harvest due to poor storage.' Then the solution: how your product or service fixes it. Follow with the market size: show you've done the math, e.g., 'There are 1.5 million smallholder farmers in Kenya; we target 5% in year one.' Include a slide on your business model: how you make money. Then traction: any sales, partnerships, or pilot results. Next, competition: who else is doing this and why you're different. Then your team: why you are the right people. Add financial projections: 3-year revenue and profit forecast. Finally, the ask: how much you need and what you'll use it for. Use tools like Canva or PowerPoint. Keep text minimalâuse images, charts, and icons. For African contexts, use local photos and examples. Practice your 10-minute pitch. Your deck should stand alone without you, but with you, it should tell a story. Remember, investors invest in people and clarity, not just ideas.

lessons.title: Storytelling for Impact
lessons.body: Numbers alone don't move people; stories do. In Africa, storytelling is part of our cultureâuse it in your pitch. Start with a personal anecdote: why did you start this business? For example, 'When I was 12, my mother's maize crop failed because she couldn't afford fertilizer. That's why I founded AgriBoost.' This creates emotional connection. Then introduce a character: a customer or beneficiary. Describe their struggle and how your business changed their life. Use sensory details: 'Fatima, a tomato seller in Kano, used to lose half her stock daily. Now with our solar-powered cooler, she saves 80% and doubled her income.' Keep it under 2 minutes. Structure: hook, problem, solution, result. Use simple language, avoid jargon. Practice with a timer. In pitches, alternate between story and data: story for emotion, data for credibility. For African audiences, use proverbs or local metaphors. For international investors, explain local context briefly. Tools: record yourself on your phone, watch it, and refine. A good story makes your pitch memorable. Investors hear many pitches; the one with a human story stands out. Remember, your story should align with your business mission. Don't exaggerate; authenticity wins. After telling a story, link it back to your business metrics: 'That's why we've grown 20% month-on-month.' This blends heart and head.

lessons.title: Public Speaking and Delivery Skills
lessons.body: Great content fails with poor delivery. In Africa, where respect and connection matter, your body language and voice are key. First, practice your pitch aloud at least 10 times. Record yourself and watch for filler words ('um', 'uh') and nervous habits. Stand tall, make eye contact with different people in the audience. Use hand gestures to emphasize points. Speak slowly and clearlyâmany African audiences include non-native English speakers, so clarity helps. Pause after key points to let them sink in. Vary your tone: don't be monotone. Smile when appropriate. If you're nervous, take deep breaths before you start. Arrive early, test your slides and microphone. Dress professionally but comfortablyâin many African contexts, a neat shirt or dress is fine. Move around if you can, but don't pace. Use the stage: walk to the screen to point at a chart. For virtual pitches, look at the camera, not the screen. Keep your energy high. Practice with a friend who gives honest feedback. Join a local Toastmasters club if available. Remember, confidence comes from preparation. Even if you make a mistake, continue. The audience wants you to succeed. After your pitch, ask for feedback. Over time, you'll improve. Your delivery can make or break your pitch, so invest time in it.

lessons.title: Handling Q&A Sessions
lessons.body: The Q&A after your pitch is where investors test your knowledge and passion. Prepare for common questions: How do you make money? Who are your competitors? What's your customer acquisition cost? What are the risks? How will you use the funds? Know your numbers cold. In Africa, investors may ask about regulatory hurdles, currency fluctuations, or logistics. Have answers ready. When asked a question, listen fully, then repeat it to ensure understanding. Take a moment to think before answering. If you don't know, say 'I don't know, but I'll find out and get back to you.' Never bluff. For tough questions, stay calm and confident. If someone is hostile, don't argue; acknowledge their concern and explain your perspective. Use the Q&A to reinforce your key messages. For example, if asked about competition, highlight your unique advantage. Keep answers conciseâ30 seconds to 1 minute. If a question is too detailed, offer to discuss offline. Bring supporting documents or a one-pager with key metrics. Practice Q&A with a mentor or team. Record your practice sessions. In group pitches, decide who answers what. After the session, note down questions you struggled with and prepare better answers for next time. Good Q&A can turn a lukewarm pitch into a funded deal.

lessons.title: Customizing Pitches for Different Audiences
lessons.body: Different audiences care about different things. Investors want returns, scalability, and exit potential. Banks want collateral, cash flow, and repayment ability. Grant organizations want social impact, sustainability, and alignment with their mission. Customers want benefits and price. In Africa, you might pitch to local angel investors, international VCs, government agencies, or development banks. Each requires a tailored pitch. For investors, emphasize market size, traction, and financial projections. For banks, focus on your business's stability, assets, and repayment plan. For grantors, highlight job creation, women's empowerment, or environmental impact. For customers, talk about how your product solves their problem. Adjust your language: with local audiences, use local examples and maybe a local language greeting. With international audiences, explain the African context briefly and avoid assuming they know your market. Your slide deck can have a core set of slides, but you can swap in audience-specific slides. For example, for impact investors, add a slide on social metrics. For a bank, add a slide on collateral. Practice your pitch for each audience. If you have 5 minutes, cut to the essentials. If you have 20 minutes, go deeper. Research your audience beforehand: who are they? What have they funded before? What are their pet peeves? Tailoring shows respect and increases your chances. Don't use a one-size-fits-all pitch.

lessons.title: Mock Pitch Practice
lessons.body: Mock pitches are rehearsals that prepare you for the real thing. Organize a session with friends, mentors, or fellow entrepreneurs. Set up a room like a real pitch: a projector, a timer, and an audience. Invite 3-5 people who can give honest feedback. Ask them to play different roles: one skeptical investor, one friendly supporter, one who asks detailed financial questions. Deliver your full pitch, including slides and Q&A. Record it on your phone. Afterward, ask for feedback on clarity, delivery, and content. Did you explain your business model clearly? Was your story compelling? Did you handle questions well? Note areas for improvement. Repeat the mock pitch at least three times, refining each time. In Africa, you can also join pitch competitions or incubator programs that offer practice. For virtual pitches, test your internet, camera, and lighting. Practice with a timer: most pitches are 5-10 minutes. If you go over, cut content. After each mock, update your slides and script. Get feedback from someone who doesn't know your businessâthey'll spot confusing parts. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become. Remember, even Steve Jobs rehearsed extensively. Mock pitches turn nervousness into readiness. After a few rounds, you'll be ready to impress real investors.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pitching and Presenting Your Business Plan

A business plan that stays in a drawer creates no value. In African agribusiness, the pitch is often the moment when an idea becomes finance, a partnership, or a market order. This practical reference consolidates the essentials from the moduleâbuilding a pitch deck, storytelling, delivery, Q&A handling, audience customisation, and mock practiceâinto a single working document you can use before any investor meeting, grant panel, or buyer negotiation.

Treat this as an operating manual, not theory. The numbers, tables, and checklist below are drawn from African agribusiness realities: thin working capital, seasonal cash flows, fragmented value chains, and investors who need confidence that you can execute under pressure.

1. Creating a Pitch Deck That Works in African Agribusiness

Your deck is a support tool, not a script. Investors in African agriculture typically see dozens of decks per cycle. The ones that move forward share a common trait: they answer the investor's core questionâcan this team convert this opportunity into cash flow and impact?âwithin the first three slides.

A standard 10â12 slide structure works across most contexts: title, problem, solution, market opportunity, business model, traction, competition, team, financials, the ask, and impact. For agribusiness specifically, add a slide on seasonality and working capital. Maize, cocoa, coffee, and horticulture businesses all face harvest-cycle cash gaps. If your deck does not explain how you survive the lean months, you have not explained your business.

Use local currency and USD equivalents. Show unit economics per hectare, per tonne, or per farmer. A poultry venture that cannot state cost per bird and margin per cycle will not survive due diligence.

2. Storytelling for Impact

Data convinces; stories move. The strongest agribusiness pitches open with a specific person or placeâa smallholder in Meru, a cooperative in Ogun State, a cold-chain gap in Tamaleâthen zoom out to the market. This is not sentimentality; it is framing. Investors need to see the human problem your business solves because that is where the demand lives.

Structure your narrative in three acts: tension (the problem and why it persists), transformation (what your business changes), and evidence (traction, numbers, contracts). Keep the story under 90 seconds. Then let the deck carry the detail.

3. Public Speaking and Delivery Skills

Delivery is trainable. The main failure modes in African pitch competitions and investor rooms are: speaking too fast, reading slides, apologising for the business, and failing to land the ask. Address each directly.

Practice standing, with a timer, without notes for the first three minutes. Record yourself on a phone. Watch for filler words and downward inflection at the end of sentences. Speak to the back of the room. Pause after key numbersâsilence signals confidence.

If presenting in a second language, simplify sentence structure rather than memorising complex phrasing. Clarity beats sophistication. If presenting virtually, test your connection, lighting, and audio before the session; connectivity failures have killed otherwise strong pitches.

4. Handling Q&A Sessions

Q&A is where pitches are won or lost. Investors test whether you understand your numbers and whether you are honest about risk. Prepare answers for the ten most likely questions: unit economics, customer acquisition, regulatory risk, currency exposure, team gaps, competition, use of funds, repayment or exit, climate risk, and what happens if the raise fails.

Use a simple method: acknowledge, answer, evidence, stop. Do not ramble. If you do not know, say so and offer to follow up with data. Investors respect that more than invented numbers.

5. Customising Pitches for Different Audiences

The same business needs different pitches for different rooms. A commercial bank wants repayment capacity and collateral. An impact fund wants measurable social outcomes alongside returns. A grant panel wants alignment with development priorities. A buyer wants supply reliability, quality, and price. A government agency wants jobs, food security, and tax revenue.

Build one master deck, then create audience-specific versions by reordering slides and adjusting the ask. Never deliver the same pitch to a bank and an impact investor; it signals you do not understand your audience.

6. Mock Pitch Practice

Rehearse under realistic pressure. Recruit three people: one who knows your sector, one who knows finance, and one who knows nothing about your business. Present to each. The sector expert will probe operations; the finance person will attack numbers; the outsider will expose jargon. Fix what they surface.

Run at least three full mock pitches before a real meeting. Time them. Record them. Review them. The goal is not perfection; it is eliminating avoidable errors.

Data Table 1: Typical Investor Questions and What They Signal

Question What the investor is testing Strong answer includes
What are your unit economics? Whether you understand profitability per unit Cost per unit, price, margin, assumptions
How do you handle seasonality? Working capital and cash-flow discipline Harvest calendar, credit terms, storage plan
Who is your customer and why will they buy? Market validation and demand realism Named buyers, contracts, repeat orders
What is your competitive advantage? Defensibility and execution capability Supply relationships, logistics, certifications
What happens if this raise fails? Risk awareness and resilience Lean plan, bridge options, cost cuts
How will you measure impact? Accountability and reporting capacity Farmer numbers, income change, tonnage

Source: Adapted from Root Capital, Investor Pitch Guide for Agricultural SMEs (2021), and Acumen, Lean Data for Impact practitioner notes.

Data Table 2: Audience Customisation Matrix

Audience Primary interest Lead with Avoid
Commercial bank Repayment capacity Cash flow, collateral, track record Impact language without numbers
Impact investor Return + measurable impact Unit economics + farmer outcomes Vague social claims
Grant panel Development alignment Jobs, food security, SDG link Commercial jargon
Offtaker / buyer Supply reliability Volume, quality, delivery schedule Funding ask
Government agency Jobs, tax, food security Local employment, compliance Criticism of policy
Cooperative / farmers Fair price, input access Transparent pricing, support services Complex financial structures

Source: Compiled from AGRA, Access to Finance for Smallholder Agriculture (2022), and IFC, Agribusiness Investment Climate guidance.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Financial and Legal Accuracy

Never present financial projections, land ownership documents, or regulatory approvals you cannot substantiate. In several African jurisdictions, misrepresenting financials to secure investment or grants can constitute fraud under national securities and anti-corruption laws. Always verify tax registration, cooperative agreements, and export certifications before pitching. If you are unsure about a legal claim in your deck, remove it or state it as an assumption. Investors conduct due diligence; a single false claim can end the relationship and damage your reputation across the sector.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Problem is specific and quantified â name the region, crop, and scale of the gap.
  2. Solution has unit economics â cost, price, margin, and assumptions are stated.
  3. Traction is evidenced â revenue, contracts, pilot results, or farmer numbers.
  4. The ask is exact â amount, use of funds, timeline, and expected outcome.
  5. Seasonality and working capital are addressed â show how you survive lean months.
  6. Deck is customised to the audience â bank, impact fund, grant, or buyer version.
  7. Q&A answers are rehearsed â ten likely questions, honest answers, no invention.
  8. Three mock pitches completed â timed, recorded, and reviewed with feedback.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Root Capital â Agricultural SME Finance Resources â investor pitch guides and rural enterprise toolkits.
  • IFC Agribusiness â Investment and Advisory Publications â market studies and investment climate reports.
  • AGRA â African Agriculture Finance and Policy Reports â smallholder finance and value chain analysis.
  • FAO Smallholder and Family Farming Resources â data and guidance on African agricultural systems.
  • Acumen â Lean Data and Impact Measurement Guides â practical impact reporting for social enterprises.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Use this reference before every pitch, and update it as your business and audience evolve.

quiz.q: What is the ideal number of slides for a pitch deck?
quiz.explanation: A pitch deck should be concise, typically 10-12 slides to keep the audience engaged.

quiz.q: Which slide should come immediately after the problem slide?
quiz.explanation: After stating the problem, you present your solution to show how you address it.

quiz.q: What is a key element to include in the 'ask' slide?
options: B) How much money you need and its use
C) A list of all competitors
quiz.explanation: The ask slide specifies the funding amount and how it will be used.

quiz.q: Why is storytelling important in a pitch?
options: D) It impresses with big words
quiz.explanation: Stories create emotional connections that make your pitch memorable.

quiz.q: What structure should a pitch story follow?
quiz.explanation: A good story starts with a hook, presents the problem, offers a solution, and shows the result.

quiz.q: How long should a pitch story ideally be?
quiz.explanation: A pitch story should be concise, typically under 2 minutes, to maintain attention.

quiz.q: What is a recommended technique to improve public speaking delivery?
options: A) Speak as fast as possible
quiz.explanation: Recording yourself helps identify areas for improvement in delivery.

quiz.q: Why is eye contact important during a pitch?
options: A) It shows you memorized your script
B) It builds connection with the audience
D) It helps you see the clock
quiz.explanation: Eye contact builds trust and connection with your audience.

quiz.q: What should you do if you make a mistake during your pitch?
quiz.explanation: Continuing confidently shows professionalism and keeps the pitch on track.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy for handling a question you don't know the answer to?
options: B) Admit you don't know and offer to follow up
quiz.explanation: Honesty and a commitment to follow up maintain credibility.

quiz.q: How long should your answer to a Q&A question typically be?
quiz.explanation: Concise answers of 30 seconds to 1 minute keep the session efficient.

quiz.q: What should you do before a Q&A session to prepare?
options: B) Know your numbers and anticipate common questions
D) Let your team handle everything
quiz.explanation: Knowing your key metrics and anticipating questions builds confidence.

quiz.q: Which audience is most interested in social impact?
quiz.explanation: Grant organizations typically prioritize social impact and mission alignment.

quiz.q: What should you emphasize when pitching to a bank?
quiz.explanation: Banks focus on repayment ability, which is supported by collateral and cash flow.

quiz.q: Why is customizing your pitch important?
options: A) It shows respect and increases relevance
C) It allows you to use the same slides
quiz.explanation: Tailoring your pitch to the audience's interests makes it more relevant and effective.

quiz.q: What is a mock pitch?
options: A) A fake pitch to trick investors
B) A practice pitch with feedback
quiz.explanation: A mock pitch is a rehearsal to practice and receive feedback before the real pitch.

quiz.q: How many times should you ideally practice your mock pitch?
quiz.explanation: Practicing at least three times helps refine your pitch and build confidence.

quiz.q: What should you do after a mock pitch?
options: B) Ask for feedback and refine
quiz.explanation: Feedback is valuable for improving your pitch for the real thing.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of mock pitches?
options: C) They replace the need for a business plan
D) They are only for beginners
quiz.explanation: Mock pitches help you become more comfortable and confident.

quiz.q: In a pitch deck, what should the traction slide show?
options: B) Sales, partnerships, or pilot results
quiz.explanation: Traction demonstrates market validation and progress.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in pitch decks?
quiz.explanation: Too much text overwhelms the audience; slides should be visual and concise.

quiz.q: How can you make your pitch story more relatable?
options: B) Use a real customer example
quiz.explanation: A real customer example makes the story tangible and relatable.

quiz.q: What is one way to practice public speaking?
options: C) Only practice in your head
quiz.explanation: Toastmasters provides a supportive environment to practice speaking.

quiz.q: What should you do if an investor asks a hostile question?
options: B) Stay calm and acknowledge their concern
quiz.explanation: Staying calm and addressing the concern professionally maintains credibility.

quiz.q: What is a good way to handle a detailed question that requires more time?
options: A) Answer fully on the spot
quiz.explanation: Offering to discuss offline keeps the Q&A focused and shows willingness to engage.

quiz.q: Why should you research your audience before pitching?
options: A) To tailor your pitch to their interests
B) To impress them with your knowledge
quiz.explanation: Understanding your audience allows you to customize your pitch for maximum impact.

quiz.q: What should you include in a pitch to impact investors?
quiz.explanation: Impact investors care about social and environmental metrics.

quiz.q: What is a key element of a mock pitch session?
quiz.explanation: Using a timer helps you practice keeping within time limits.

quiz.q: How can you get the most out of a mock pitch?
options: A) Invite people who don't know your business
quiz.explanation: People unfamiliar with your business can spot confusing parts.

quiz.q: What should you do if you go over time during a mock pitch?
quiz.explanation: Cutting content ensures you stay within the time limit and keep your pitch focused.
